children.title: Types of freedom in the Montessori environment

blocks.text: Freedom to move

Within the Montessori classroom, children are free to move around the room, and move from one activity to the next. Children who move around the room are more likely to choose purposeful work when they have fulfilled their need for activity. In consequence, by allowing freedom of movement, children learn to explore their environment; and therefore discover their interests.
Freedom of choice

Freedom of choice is fundamental to the Montessori approach. This is because choice allows children to discover their needs, interests and abilities. Furthermore, freedom of choice encourages children to be engaged in their learning, and thus discover the outcome of the activity.
Freedom of time

Freedom of time allows children to work with the same material for as long as they like. In effect, this encourages children to learn at their own pace, develop the skills of concentration, and learn patience to wait their turn.
Freedom to repeat

The three-hour work cycle gives students the opportunity to work with materials and achieve success through practice. Furthermore, through repetition, children learn to self-correct and problem solve.
Freedom to communicate
Montessori encourages communication in the classroom. Children learn to discuss activities, problem solve, and develop their social skills.
Freedom to make mistakes

Furthermore, the design of the Montessori materials encourages children to discover the outcome of the activity by themselves. Each material is designed with a visual control of error. This guides the child to understand the outcome of the activity through hands-on learning experiences.
Freedom to reflect
The children should be allowed to take a break from their work and have their own time to reflect.

The rules in the classroom have to be clear, easy to remember and to be based on some strong motivations that the children can easily understand. The rules of the environment should not feel for the children that reflect only the will of the adult, but they have help the children understand how they benefit or protect the members of the group.

In the Elementary classroom there are more possibilities for freedom as the children can work in groups and it is also a time with a sensibility for the moral values. The guide has the responsibility to help the children develop their social skills and this can be done not only through the lessons of grace and courtesy but also by involving the children to collaborate with as many companions as possible in the classroom.
“The child who has never learned to work by himself to set goals for his own acts or to be the master of this own will it is recognizable in the adult who lets other guide

him and feels a constant need of the others.” Maria Montessori The children have to learn to be responsible for their own work. In order to do so they need to learn what are the appropriate challenges for them, to learn the value of the time, to appreciate how long a work might take them and to understand that once you start a work you should finish it. All these can be acquired through the practice with the materials. The moral responsibility it is also very important has to be supported from an early age especially in the second plane of development where they are sensitivity to morality and in a continuous search for what it is fair or not. The responsibility for one’s actions it is an important component of the discipline and freedom. The children should learn to be responsible for their actions, however not

with a goal of making them feel guilty but to help them regulate their actions and learn from their own experiences. The independence it has to be conquered by the child and it can be offered to his as a gift by no one.
The second plane children need to learn about how society functions and to understand that the school does not contain all the answers and solutions.
Going out is the activity in which a child or a group of children can leave the environment with a question/quest to find an answer in the public library, museum or the workshop of a specialist.
For going out it is very important to make sure to study the local legislation to make sure that the parents agree with their children going out by themselves.
The children have to prepare their own visit by first calling and setting up an appointment. After setting the appointment they should prepare their itinerary and the questions they want to ask.
After the visit the children should make sure to send a thank you card to the place that they visited.
If the children going out are a larger group, they can share the tasks (e.g. some can be in charge of the appointment, some of the itinerary and so on).

The cosmic fables are also known as the great stories or great lessons. The cosmic fables and the key lessons are the very important in the Montessori education. The lessons are not similar to the ones in traditional schools, the knowledge is offered through key lessons (presentations) and the cosmic fables.
There are six cosmic fables in the Montessori Elementary and have the role to feed the imagination and arouse the interest of the child.
God who has no hands (Geography)
This story opens up the Cosmic Education presenting to the children the whole known to the human beings: the universe
The elements (cosmic agents) of the story are the sun, land, water and air
This first cosmic fable tells the story of the creation of the universe and the planet preparing for the next one
Story of life (Biology)
It provides an overview of the creation of life on the planet Earth
The elements (cosmic agents) of the story are plants, animals, human beings
The story takes the child into a journey from the apparition of the first cells until the arrival of the human beings
Coming of the human beings (History)
The story talks about the gifts of the human beings: capacity to think/wonder, the special love(empathy) and usage of the hands to work
Story of the Ox and the House (Language)
The story presents the evolution of the written language and the long journey the humanity has taken until reaching to the present alphabet.

It helps the children become aware of the language, its use and history. This story helps the children develop an appreciation for the written language and the magical powers that gave to the humanity to transmit thoughts, knowledge and write their history.
Story of Numbers (Mathematics)

This story take the children on a journey to discover the hard work that has been carried out by many generations to create a numerical system which is easy to use. The discovery of the decimal system and the numbers as we know them today opened the gate of mathematics.
Great River (Biology)
This cosmic story it is introduced in the second cycle.
“If we follow these particularities, we find that it is possible to give our ideas to children. If we use the method used by the fairy tales, we can get into

communication with the mind of the child. So instead of giving just any teaching we must prepare short stories along these lines. They must have a few, clearly drawn persons with unusual characteristics. There must be a limited environment full of attractive and new things, because the children's interest is in the fantastic side, in

the unusual. Children can reconstruct every story, but they also like something that is connected with movement and a real environment. They like something they can handle so that they can fix the idea in their minds. This may be a projection of something that is inside; they construct with blocks and sand, let them construct in relation to what they have in their minds, give them something new which is in line with their natural psychology. Children can take from the environment without a teacher. This is their natural capacity. They also have a capacity for work, which stimulates their minds. We have studied these facts before,' now we must see that children also have the capacity to take from stories told by an adult. We can give them stories which are like fairy tales and give knowledge under the guide of these stories. We can give history for example. The difference between history and fairy tales is that history is facts and fairy tales are invented. History is facts, but the facts are far away from us and it is fantastic. We cannot see it, we can only imagine it. History can be an exercise for imaginative construction. You cannot impart it through the senses but only through the imagination. The children must reconstruct the details. The story of the past can be just a boring account of events. It must not

be given in this way. It must be given like a fairy tale. The stories must be short, with a few well-drawn characters; the environment must be limited, unusual and very clear. They must all be built around something fantastic. History can show an environment
which is very different from our own.” Maria Montessori – The child, society and the world – page 47

The cosmic fables presents the whole and orient the child in what he can explore. The first five cosmic fables are given very early in the school year, in the first months and in a sequence meanwhile the sixth cosmic fable of the “Great River” is given later, usually in the second cycle.
Giving the whole framework of their studies, it helps the children feel orientate and empowers them to take initiative.

The cosmic fables can be announced beforehand and as these are a group activity for the classroom it allows them to prepare themselves for the day. Most of the cosmic fables with the exception of one have material to accompany them (charts, timelines, etc.)

The fables should not be broken into different pieces and a good story telling capacity from the guide is important to make sure that the cosmic fable transmits the message clearly. The story should use precise language with beautiful metaphors with the goal to transmit the information accurate and attractive for the respective age group.

The children should be given the necessary time to absorb the story without having the adults question them or assign tasks after the cosmic fable was told. After a cosmic fable has been told there is a time for questions, talk on the subject or even debate.
The cosmic fables in the second cycle can be enriched with more scientifically facts to appeal to the interest of the child in the second cycle.
The cosmic fables should be presented at the beginning of the school year, however the guide should not rush to give them too close to each other.

The key lesson we can think of as the presentations given to the children in the Montessori classroom. The key lessons pick up details from the cosmic fables and bring new details to the children. The presentations are given individually and in small groups. A presentation should be clear and lead the children to work by themselves.

It is very important to understand that the key lessons, or presentations, should be guiding the child in the work that there is to do however should never explain everything as the small discoveries that the children can make in the work are the catalyst for further independent work.
The key lessons are the minimum necessary to start the children working with a concept and from where they can do more of their own discoveries.
Key Lessons include the following
Arithmetic – large bead frame – the Key to category multiplication, ten and the powers of ten, the key is given with the work on the notation paper first
Biology – needs, function, relationship with environment
Geography – rotation and revolution are keys to the Earth’s movements
History – Fundamental needs of Humans, Key to time with the Black Strip and Hand Time-Line
Geometry – key to making abstractions through manipulatory activity, e.g. congruency, similarity and equivalence
Language -Word Study, is a key to how it changes and grows

Individual lesson should be given only to the children that struggle with a particular aspect (e.g. spelling). The individual lessons should be short, on the specific topic and should guide the child to overcome by himself the difficulty encountered.
“It is not the Montessori method that gave birth to the first Children’s House, the first Children’s House gave birth to the Montessori Method.“ Salvatore Vallitutti
Evolution of the Montessori Method:
1907 – The first Children’s House opened in Via Marsi, 58 in Rome

The centre is opened as a day-care centre for the poor children in the neighbourhood. Maria Montessori was the supervisor of the project and had another person in the school on a daily basis. This first project allows her to make a series of discoveries that slowly become the basis of what later becomes the method that we know today. The method it has always been experimental with constant revisions over the time. The discoveries made where related to the natural behaviour of the children towards their own development and independence in the environment. (E.g. their sensibility for order related to the desire of independence, the repetition, the work with concentration all for their own development). The parents of these children asked Maria Montessori if she could help their children to read and write. At first hesitant, Maria Montessori started a program for reading and writing. This proved to be a real success with the children starting to write before reading, a series of events that made this experimental start famous around Italy and soon around Europe.
1909 – The Franchetti family invites Maria Montessori in Villa Montesca, Umbria

Maria Montessori is invited to write down about her discoveries in the Children’s House in Rome. The original title did not include her name, however the publishers for the English language version include her name as the original one was too long. Maria Montessori starts to study her predecessors Itard and Seguin. She has a high interest in the work of Seguin, she translates his book from French and applies his method in her first work with challenged children.
The first training course it is hold at Villa Montesca.
1916 – The book “Advanced Method” it is published by Maria Montessori

The book it is called the “L’autoeducazione nelle scuole elementare”, a rough translation can be “The self-education in primary school”. The book it is published in Italian as a single book. Maria Montessori says that this book it is a continuation of the first book. In English it is separated in two volumes: “Spontaneous activity in education” and “Montessori Elementary material”. The second volume includes work for Language, Arithmetic, Geometry, Music and Art. This book remains relevant for the language part and the music.
Maria Montessori’s mother dies and her son Mario Montessori comes to live with her.
The first international Montessori Course it is given in Rome.
There are later courses given all over the world. E.g. Every two years a course in London.
1929 – The AMI is being founded to safeguard the values of the method.
Mario Montessori is setting up the association and Maria Montessori becomes president.
Early 1930’s – Maria Montessori moves to Barcelona in Spain

The Secret of childhood and the psycho-books come all out from the time she lived in Spain: Psychoarithmetic, Psychogrammar and Psychogeometry. In all these new books, the child is always at the centre, the development of the child. “Psycho” part in front of the subject refers that the approach places the child at the centre and not the subject itself. The idea was that you can take a subject apart and offer it to children at the appropriate time according to their developmental needs. For example geometry it is offered in the Children’s House as a sensorial material as it appeals to their sensitivities. It is used there to develop the senses and the shapes are absorbed by the young child. We can think of the geometry in the Children’s House as a Hidden geometry. Later in the Elementary the work of geometry should be a work of discovery for the children. The materials are very important as their precision it is crucial for leaving the correct impressions for the child and lead the child to discoveries.
1936 – Maria Montessori leaves Spain as Civil war breaks out, she gets to Holland

She get a school in Laren, Holland with a 3-6, 6-9 and 9-12 environments interconnected. It becomes a good place to continue experimenting and introducing material. The materials are offered to the environment which most interest has in it. The approach had always the child at the centre.
Maria Montessori thinks that the adolescent’s studies should be more systematic at this moment.
The school in Laren it was also a training centre for adults.
In Amsterdam she gets an office where also the headquarters of AMI are.
1939 – “From Childhood to Adolescence” book is based on the talks from these years

This book has the source for the vision for the education for the adolescents. The human being during adolescence develops again in a very particular way. Maria Montessori says that during this delicate period the adolescent has to be protected in the first years of adolescence (12 – 14 years old) and only after a systematic plan of studies can be applied. Maria Montessori wanted the young adolescents to feel responsible and to have the environment to tell them what the responsibilities are. At the time she was exposing her vision the health of the adolescents was very fragile around this age so a setting in a farm it was ideal for the fresh food, the fresh air and all the responsibilities that come with all the animals at farm. Now years after, what makes an adolescent program successful it is the responsibility given to the adolescent, the opportunity to manage the project and to earn real money, therefore bringing a real value to the society.
1935 – Maria Montessori recalled that the first cornerstone of Cosmic education is laid with the course given in London

There is a talk about geology and life in this course. There is a move from the essential primary education subjects towards a more inclusive approach. It was called at first the “Telluric education”. The idea was to help the child to understand his immediate environment and the environment that was a far from the reach of the child. Later on Maria and Mario Montessori came back to the name and decided that “Cosmic Education” it was a better name to describe the work.
1930 - 1939 – The work “Education and peace” is based on speeches from these years

The word is passing through depression and fascist regimes. This Maria Montessori think that the biggest change we can bring to the world is through the children. The goal of humanity in her eyes it is not only the peace but for each individual to develop at his fullest development.
1939 – Maria Montessori arrives to India and it is forced to stay as the WWII starts

Maria Montessori writes “Creative Development in the Child” which are a reflection of the course that she gave there. The work comes in two volumes and includes the Children’s House and Elementary work, as at that time it was offered in one course. The part of the course for Elementary it was developed based on some of the questions that the children asked in that time in India. With careful observation, Maria and Mario Montessori both understood that the education had to help the “hungry mind” of the child to develop and the materials had to serve as aids for the development. Mario Montessori shared some of these questions that the children had: ”How do plants grow? They don’t eat or drink”, “How do butterflies eat? They don’t have teeth”, “Why does winter come? It is so cold”, “The Sun is so small in comparison with the Earth”. As it is clear from the children’s questions, a kind of aids to their imagination had to be created to help the children understand the universe, the live on Earth and how it was all created.
1939-1944 – “To educate human potential” book it comes out from the Kodaikanal course in India
The book it is actually published in 1946
1946 – The London Course
This course it is a reference for all the courses given today
1949 – The Montessori family returns to Italy
The course it is given in Sanremo, after the course she came to Bergamo invited by the Aligliardi family.
1950 – Maria Montessori she gives a course in Perugia
She creates the chart with the 4 planes of development
1951 – She gives the course in London
Maria Montessori creates the “Bulb” chart
1952 – Maria Montessori dies
Mario Montessori was in Africa giving a course as requested for Maria Montessori when he returns Maria Montessori already died.
1954 - 1957 – Mario Montessori starts to give seminars in different places around Europe.
Ms. Honnegar asks for help as she thinks that the course she received it wasn’t enough. Mario Montessori starts to give summer seminars with different subjects.
1956 gives a lecture about the Human Tendencies. The lecture it is printed in the booklet called “Human Tendencies and Montessori Education” by Mario Montessori
1957 - 1958 – Mario Montessori gives the second London course.
1961 – The first training centre for Elementary it is created in Bergamo.
Mario Montessori says that Maria Montessori understood that the knowledge should be presented starting with the whole and continuing until reaching the details.

The biggest whole that can be offered to the child is the Universe and the cosmic fable it is “God who has no hands” is the first one offered. Giving the whole helps the child to orientate himself and to have a framework to order his knowledge. It also helps the child to understand that everything it is presented in the whole, therefore there must be a connection.

The chart available in the booklet “The human tendencies” presents the interconnection between the non-living agents and the living agents. The non-living agents are the air, the sun, the land (rocks), and the water. The living agents are the plants, animals and human beings. There all presented on the chart with the arrows showing the interdependence.

The cosmic stories are not pointing out any idea of belonging to the whole, even so in the way they are told, they seed this ideas that will grow with the children helping them to orientate themselves.

There are six cosmic fables and “God who has no hands” the first one opens all the areas. It might be considered as an opening the story for Geography though as shown before it presents the whole and therefore it is the fable that opens all the subjects. The second cosmic fable picks up from the creation of the planet and brings the “life” into picture and its evolution in the last 500+ millions of years. We can think of this fable

as a great opening for biology and the studies that can be carried there. The next cosmic fable “The coming of the human beings” it presents the beginnings of the humanity on the planet and the special gifts the human beings came with. Another factor that made the human beings a power of change: organization and group work. This group organization it is possible due to the power of language oral and written. The fourth cosmic fable comes under the name “The story of the ox and the house” to introduce the story of the alphabet and how the human beings developed what in the western world we call the “Latin alphabet”. The fifth cosmic fable introduces the story of the numbers and it is called “The story of numbers” and shows the mathematical mind of the human beings.

The story human beings can be seen as a double agent: the adult and the child. The adult works to transform the environment and to find the comfortable and easier way to survive meanwhile the child does the developmental work to create himself and to become an adult. It is important to understand, appreciate and support this work of the child.
We can think of all the agents non-living and living and their work in this interdependence and we can talk of “Cosmic work”.
We can think as the human beings as the “Man the worker” which it can also be separated into: the transformer of the environment and the revealer.

The human beings can be characterized by the three gifts: the mind, the working hands and the love. The child uses all these three gifts to become part of the environment natural and supernature. The mind, working hands and love are the motor for his own development as well as his close relationship with the nature. The work is the force that corrects the deviations that appear in his path especially in the first plane of development.

There is a contribution of the four planes of development. In the first plane of development the child is adapting to his environment and absorbs it without judgements. It is also a great period for refining their senses and becoming “good at doing things” (Steven Huges). The work done in the first plane helps the child to be eager to work, to continue with his own development and to have good habits. It is the plane in which the children can get “normalized”. It is a creation of the self as a human being we are all born so “unfinished” in order to have this power of adaptability.

In the second plane of development the characteristics of the child are his “hungry mind” for the acquisition of knowledge, an imagination that comes in the help of the senses to understand better the environment that surrounds him at a micro and macro level. A sensitivity for the moral aspects (morality) of the immediate environment becomes evident and the child becomes very interested in what is correct, incorrect, inappropriate or appropriate. The work of this sensitivity conducts to the building of a personal code of ethics. The social aspect of the child in this plane of development it is not a sensitivity, as the tendency to associate it is characteristic for the human beings in general. However in the second plane of development this tendency it is present in the form of association with other children of their own age group. One can think of this association as a mini-society in which the children try to be the owners of their

decisions. If we take all these characteristics together we can observe the child in the second plane of development as being very interested in the humanity, the work that has been carried, how this work impacted their life and how this work can be carried out in the future. The second plane child works in conscious way, a work to satisfy his own hungry mind and that makes him a worthy member of the groups that he has formed. With work and responsibility a love towards the universe, the life and humanity is developed and together with this a sense of human solidarity that links them to the cosmic work that it is taking place.

Montessori acknowledged with Homo sapiens a new form of life appeared, that is we are not born with a set of instincts that make individuals act like their species, we have a psychic need that needs to be met through education. But it can’t be any old education, but it has to be an education that allows each individual to develop in the way it was intended for them. The Montessori education it can be considered as an aid to life.
“We should like to mention the important contribution by Maria Montessori made by discovering the psychic phenomenon in the construction of the child, it was this
discovery which made her create an environment allowing the child full scope for his development by providing the necessary material with the freedom he needs for
constructive activities” Mario Montessori
The components of the Montessori approach are
The prepared environment
Physical environment  Motives for activity
Social environment  Adult and other children
The human tendencies
The mathematical mind
The sensitivities according to the four planes of development
The prepared environment should support the developmental needs of each plane.

For the children from 0 to 3, we can think of the child spending time in the family, from 3-6 there is the Children’s House, from 6-12 there is the Elementary and the Cosmic education, from 12 to 18 Erdkinder and from 18 to 24 the university. The physical environment it is especially important in the first and third planes of development, however in all the children the Montessori environment should present motives for activity.
There are two pillars of the Montessori approach: the prepared environment and the limited intervention of the adult.
Respect for the child

The unique developmental needs and interests of each child are respected. Children are not compared based on merit, they are valued for their individuality. Montessori education embraces multiple styles and pathways to learning, and understands that each child’s early learning journey is different.
Sensitive Periods

The Montessori learning environment supports these periods by proving children with hands-on learning experiences that encourage repetition and problem solving to maximise learning during these windows of opportunity.
The Absorbent Mind

The first six years of life are crucial in a child’s development as they establish an understanding of themselves and their world. The Montessori environment supports children in this task by providing them with learning experiences that promote their sense of belonging, confidence, independence and agency.
Teaching Roles

Children are the centre of the Montessori classroom. The role of the teacher is to observe and guide, being mindful of children’s changing interests, developmental needs, and emotions. Teachers plan daily lessons for each child.
Montessori Materials

Montessori materials are sensory-based learning tools that are designed to isolate one skill or concept. The materials encourage hands-on learning, independent problem solving, and analytical thinking. Especially unique, is that each Montessori material is designed with a visual control of error.
“These materials are a teacher, that is always ready, that are always constant in patience and constant of mood. Materials that permit analysis and discoveries until
the core or heart of the problem is reached. It is a teacher that never tires, a teacher that offers and supplies prompt correction, that is objective, that revises the

work without trauma or tiring the child it is a material that permits abstract relationships transformed into direct perception, materials that require constant research of similarities and differences permits classification, permits use of patterns
as helpful organising a reasoned out sequence for instance square root. The material which is for working with, it is for development which is not there for didactic

help because it is made for the child so that the child can understand particular solutions and procedures and so the child can reach solutions and build procedure with the slowness and laboriousness proper to the analytical process. The material is
poly valiant because it can be used and taken up at different levels at different times, that is it can be reconsidered from different points of view by the child
themselves. It is a constructive material but it requires a creative manipulation, so it is an aid but not to the teacher it is developmental material it is designed to help the
child develop and that is why it is called development material and not didactic material.”
Preface to Psychoarithmetic, page XII Camillo Grazzini
Three Hour Work Cycle(s)
Students participate in at least one three-hour work cycle every day. This period of individual learning provides children with the opportunity to choose their work and progress at their own pace.
Normalisation
Normalisation describes the process where young children (3-6 years old) come to focus and concentrate on a task for a sustained period of time. This period of
development is characterized by: love of work, concentration, self-discipline, sociability.
Prepared Environment

The Montessori classroom is a prepared environment designed to optimise learning. Characteristics include: low open shelves, left to right display of Montessori materials in progression order, defined curriculum areas, child-sized furniture, freedom of movement, and freedom of choice.

For the second plane children the environment it is secondary, however this environment should present all the subjects related to the human knowledge. The material free the children from the adult and can be abandoned as soon as the child passes to abstraction.
The children receive key-lessons that allow them to further explore independently.
In the environment there are two kinds of aids:
For the imagination
Impressionistic
For the abstract thinking
Mathematical aids
Social environment

Maria Montessori suggested a number of 30 to 40 children in the classroom. Having a larger group it allows the children to meet other children with different characters and encourages the children to be an individual.

The children in a large get more opportunities to see work going on around them and to get inspired. They also have more opportunities to become independent. The classroom should be composed by a mixed age group with an age difference of at least 3 years for the Elementary.
The mixed age environment encourages the children to be inspired and learn from the others that are ahead instead of fostering competition.
The role of the adult

"Scientific observation then has established that education is not what the teacher gives; education is a natural process spontaneously carried out by the human individual, and is acquired not by listening to words but by experiment upon the environment. The task of the teacher becomes that of preparing a series of motives of cultural activity, spread over a specially prepared environment, and then refraining from obtrusive interference. Human teachers can only help the great work that is being done, as servants help the master. Doing so, they will be witnesses to the unfolding of the human soul and to the rising of a New Man who will not be the victim of events, but will have the clarity of vision to direct and shape the future of human society."
The first duty of the educator working with the new born or an older child is to recognize the human personality of young being and respect.
The second duty is to be a link between the child and the material.
The third duty is to protect the child’s work.

The roles of the Montessori teacher are to prepare and maintain the environment, to connect the child to the environment and to observe. It is very important to take very good care of the environment, make sure it is complete, clean and attractive for the children.

It is the task of the teacher to demonstrate to the child the use of the material and what material should be introduced to a child depending on his interests and developmental needs. Once presented the material it is important for the teacher to know when to step back and let the child work with the material independently and guard the child’s focus. The teacher must intervene when the child is misusing the material.

If in the Children’s House the role of the adult is to link the children to the material, in the Elementary it is a link of the child not only with the material buy also to the knowledge. The guide in the Elementary is also the story teller that gives to the children the vision of the whole and to support them to see that everything is inter-related, how the world functions and how cooperation made the human race thrive.
The guide should love the world, be knowledgeable, humble and be an inspiration indirectly for the children. He has a more active role

The environment should be large for the second plane children with enough space for them to work at the table as well on the floor with the materials and in groups. The environment contain only natural materials, to be clean, with natural light and access to the outdoor space where the children can continue their research, work or even rest in between works.

The responsibilities of the environment should be shared with the children and empower them to take responsibility. From the first week of school the children should understand that the environment is a part of the community.
Third plane of development

The children in the third plane of development have a strong sense of ownership. The sensitivities of the personal dignity and justice. The Erdkinder School should allow the children to do valuable work for the society and to support them to do the work by themselves. As the children pass into a plane of adolescence they require an environment in which they can apply the in the real world the things that they learn and learnt in school. Managing a farm, a small hostel or a local handcraft business prepares the children for the adult life offering them the necessary experiences for their development. As an example, the adolescents in the farm school located next to Gothenburg in Sweden, run the school by themselves only with the help of a few adults. They manage the daily duties in the farm, in the kitchen and in their residence taking responsibility for their work.

Allowing the adolescents to run a small business puts them in contact with the real life challenges, they learn to manage their budget and to bring innovative ideas into being that might surprise even the long established businesses. Giving the trust and

responsibility to a young adult that seeks to satisfy his personal dignity is important and too often forgotten by traditional educational system that treats the students in a linear way during the whole educational program.

The children have journals to make sure that they write that they have done during the day, allowing them to reflect on the usage of the day. The older children can look back at the activities that they have done and record also their impressions about their work.

The guide helps the children cover all the subjects during the school year and makes sure that a child is not falling behind on the long run. This can be done by working with the strengths of the child in some subjects.

The guide should also have short conferences with the students from time to time to make sure that they are on track with their work. This conferences can be daily, weekly or even monthly depending on each child and they progress in the classroom.
The children should feel independent and with the passage of the time they should know how to choose an activity, look for help from various sources and help the others become independent as well.
The guide should be aware of the space available in the environment and practice to be able to offer presentations which are clear, organized and easy to follow by the children.

The guide should make sure that he understands well what work it is developmentally appropriate for the child at a certain point in his development. This understanding can be acquired by observation, by having a strong knowledge of the human tendencies and sensitivities.
The guide should have a weekly report of all the presentation that were given during the week.
The guide can prepare monthly reports for each child with all the presentations given and with the child’s progress.
When the children arrive to a new environment they have to be helped to be orientated and to learn the rules of the environment.

The guide at the beginning of the year how they would like their community to be. It is important to involve the children in establishing their community rules. The rules of the community should be simple to remember and have to be followed by all the members (adults and children).

The guides have to ensure that they are not working in isolation to the rest of the school community so it is important to have a calendar that has school wide events and class events that may or may not include the parents.
Work cycle and classroom management
It is recommendable, if possible, to let the children tidy up their works only at the end of the day instead of doing it twice (lunch and afternoon)
Science has showed that the human brain for some individuals works best in the afternoon, having an afternoon work cycle might be beneficial for some of the children
The sessions with the specialist teachers are best to be organized in the afternoon after the scheduled work cycle so it won’t interfere with the daily routine of the children.
It is very important to observe each child individually and to understand his work patterns, when he concentrates and allow him to work when he can do it with the maximum involvement
Parent education
Help them understand what the Montessori Method is all about.
The parents must have clear how this educational method works in order to be able to cooperate with the school during the educational process.
Parent meetings and conferences are a great tool to communicate with the parents.
Have observation days for the parents.
During the school year you can organize days when the children can prepare presentations for their parents.
A good book to read for the parents is:Angeline Stoll Lillard – The Science behind the Genius
Important both for teachers and parents: Never underestimate children.
Prepared environment
Environment: Break it up into several spaces with shelves.
Set up a permanent history corner where you exchange things
You can have different things in the classroom which are not Montessori materials, but don't keep them as permanent materials.
Have a quiet place or a quiet corner where the children can go and calm down.
Use indoor shoes for the teachers and the students.
Limited interventions of the teacher
Create a connection with the child so he can feel free to express his emotions.
The adult should not manipulate the child. It is very important that the communication with the child to be clear, honest and direct.
Flexibility and justice/regulations
Don’t force the child to remove something, ex. a hat that he feels secure wearing. Help the child so that he gives it up himself.
We have to allow for things that are temporary, for e.g. items that might make the child feel safe and secure at the beginning of the school or after a hard emotional time for him.
There has to be exceptions for rules. Distributive justice is not true justice.
The environment should have clear regulations that are followed not only by the children but also by the adults present.
School standards for AMI USA
Teachers and assistants
1 AMI trained teacher in the classroom
Optional: 1 non-teaching assistants (can vary depending on country) – should be complementary to the teacher (maybe have some qualities that the teacher doesn’t have)
Full set of materials – AMI approved manufacturer
Number of students
Good balance of students according to age/gender
Appropriate number of students
Nido (2 months up to walking): 6 to 9 children
IC (walking – 3 ): 10-14 children
CASA (3-6): 24 – 35 children
Elementary (6-9/ 9-12 /6-12): 24-35 children
Work time
Elementary: minimum 3 hours – every morning / 2-3 hours in the afternoon
Cursive and script

Cursive writing should come first as it helps the development of the brain and it is linked to the sensitive period for the movement of the hand. Print can be learned in parallel as it required to read most of the books. For practicing the writing at the beginning it is ideal if a board can be used so the child can erase the letters that he doesn’t like and try again without frustration.

Cursive letters also help the children at the beginning to write the words with the necessary space as in each separate word the letters are linked, the space representing only the passage to a new word.
There are many paper linking cursive writing with the brain development as it thought that when writing in cursive you use both sides of the brain.
Challenged children
Maximum 10 % of the classroom – maximum 1 with a certain problem.
Specialist teachers
In the afternoon after the work cycle if required.
The specialist can be available on a specific time and the children can choose when to go in that time frame.
Help the specialist to learn more about the Montessori Method if they are interested to teach in a Montessori school.
Concentrated work
The concentrated work is linked with the constancy of the environment and with the avoidance of the distractions.
Independence vs. skills

Independence: to be able to function independently as an adult. It is a process of becoming independent. There are different stages of independence depending on the age of the child: functional/physical, intellectual/moral, economic, social independence.

The adult has to be an observer, to understand if a child is working in the incorrect manner, he should not leave him to figure out the answer forever alone but to give only the necessary help, punctually, when really required.
The adult’s role is to present the material and the concept in such a way that the child can work independently with the material and abandon it when he doesn’t require it anymore.
Worksheets
Only if are the initiative of the child. In the rest of the cases are not necessary.
Co-teaching
Not advisable as many conflicts can arouse especially if are trained in different places.
Language material on separated shelves or separated on the shelf
Work vs. play
The second plane children can do more work in the environment, taking care of the environment for example. The children should be given the responsibility appropriate for his age.
Work is fundamental for the development, not only for the children but also for the adults.
The humans begin working from the moment that they are born. All the work that the child does it is his work for the development.
Maria Montessori started using the word “work” for the activities of the child to help the adults understand the role of the activity for the development of the child.
The children at the beginning develop their own will, however to develop the will they need to have choice.
When the work comes from the child/nature we can think of spontaneous work.
For the pre-linguistic children the focus it is measured with their capacity to gaze at a certain point for a long time.
Work is a constructive activity.

The second plane society, there is an organization of work, establishing for themselves the rules. This organization of the work, the collective work, is the one that drives the humanity towards the development.
All the organization of work it is beneficial to satisfy in an effective way all the fundamental needs, material and spiritual.
Work is play, if play means doing something with pleasure and for an inner development.
“The mind, which receives all, does not judge, does not refuse, does not react. It absorbs everything and incarnates it in the coming man” Maria Montessori – The
Absorbent Mind

Maria Montessori used this term to describe the mind of the child during the first plane of development. She used the terms “sponge mind” to give us an idea of the mind of the child but later she corrected herself as the sponge might get saturated at some point and it is not quite right for the mind of the child (The absorbent mind retains everything, whereas a sponge that is saturated will start to lose the liquid). During the first plane, the child becomes functionally independent, develops his personality and adapts to his environment and group. Analyzing the absorbent mind helps us to understand how this process of self-construction happens.

The features of the absorbent mind can be characterized as constant and effortless absorption, there is a continuous process of absorption – whatever the experiences is the child absorbs it. This process is easy, effortless and total – it is not a hardship for the child. During this period the mind of the child is not selective, it doesn’t discriminate and everything is at equal par. Montessori spoke as well about the functioning of the mind and how it is different between birth to three and three to six years old.

In the first subdivision of the first plane of development is when the child makes his acquisitions for movement, senses and language. For the child in this subplane Maria Montessori spoke about the child as the spiritual/psychic embryo. By using this term she refers to the unique and enormous creative potential that exists in every child. Another way to describe this period is the unconscious creator. It doesn’t mean that the child is not aware in general, but that the child is not aware of the absorption in his development – the absorption isn’t a choice or an act of free will.
“The incarnate child is a spiritual embryo that must live at the expense of its
environment. Just as the physical embryo requires the special surroundings of the
womb, so the spiritual embryo also needs the protection of a living environment
warmed by love and rich in sustenance, in which everything is designed to foster its
growth and there are no obstacles on the way” Maria Montessori

During the second subplane of the first plane of development, Maria Montessori referred of the child as the conscious worker. The concept of ego appears around the age of 3 and the child will be more conscious of his preferences and starts consolidating and expanding on what has been created in the previous period (0-3). Now the absorption is enhanced by working/activity. The more the child can be independent and able to engage with the environment, the better.
It is very important to be conscious of the power of the absorbent mind. The child takes in every aspect of the environment physically and mentally like feelings,
emotions and attitudes. There are three aspects in which the child is especially sensitive: language, movement and cultural traits.

At birth the child cannot communicate but by the age of 2.5 years old the child is able to speak the language(s) of his environment. Just by being part of the environment the child develops his language(s) knowledge. The child needs the opportunity to practice both speaking and listening as absorption alone isn’t enough. The richer the language in the environment, the richer will be the child’s language. The period between birth and six years old it is the perfect period for the language acquisition. The adults should not dumb down language, for example trying to “baby talk”, as the child can absorb the language without difficulties.

When we talk about the child and the movement at this age, we are talking about the absorption of movement from the environment. Some particularities and gestures are absorbed by the child and become his way of moving, be it communication gestures or movement over different kinds of terrain. (E.g. a child that grows up in a snowy region of the globe, it will be more prepared to walk on snow/ice than a child who grew up at the tropics).
The child absorbs the cultural traits of the environment where he belongs, such as customs, greetings, food preferences, religion, values, beliefs, etc.
The child learns to love the environment where he grows in the first years of life.

“The developing child not only acquires the faculties of man: strength, intelligence, language; but, at the same time he adapts the being he is construction to the conditions of the world about him.” Maria Montessori – The absorbent mind

The work of self-construction of the child cannot be replaced by the help of the adult; the adult’s role is to create an environment that does not hinder the natural development of the child. Instead, it should offer real, enriching experiences for the child.

Maria Montessori said that she took this term “sensitive periods” from a Dutch botanist, Hugo de Vries. She wrote about this in the book Secret of Childhood. This term is now being used also by modern neuroscience.
The botanists observed these sensitive periods in the study of the butterfly, where they observed certain sensitivities of the caterpillar (where the caterpillar was drawn to light).

Maria Montessori discovered that the Human Being has as well certain innate sensitivities that draw the child to create human characteristics and functions. These innate sensitivities drive the child to interact with the environment and have a constructive role in the fundamental development of the child during the first 6 years of life.

Sensitivities have for the child a positive aspect, it means to be highly receptive to something. The sensitivities are periods which exist during a limited time span – are temporary. There is a subtle beginning, after a time the sensitivities reach a peak and then slowly fade away.
These sensitive periods are universal and are not influenced by the culture, location or beliefs of the group of people where the child is born.
As many of the sensitive periods exist and work at the same time, we might say that coexist and are overlapping.
There is an inner factor that might not be as transparent to us, as well as an outer factor which is more evident which leads to the consolidation of the inner factor.

When the child is under “a spell” of a sensitive period we often observe repetition, real focus and prolonged activity. If the child has been allowed to engage during the sensitive periods, the child will not be tired from the activity but on the contrary, he will feel refreshed. If we interrupt the child we can observe frustration, not because we stopped his activity but because we interrupted the process of construction.
The sensitive periods are highly selective and highlight certain aspects of the environment for the child’s self-construction.
We can look at the sensitive periods as windows of opportunity for the development of the child.

children.title: Sensitive periods of the first plane of development

blocks.text: The sensitive period for language ensures that the attention of the child is on human language over and above noises in the environment. The child is never ever compelled by any other sound than the sound of the human voice. The sensitivity of language is a very good example of the symbiosis between the absorbent mind and the sensitivities that ensure that the child absorbs the necessary information for his development. When we talk about adult responsibility is very important to allow the child to communicate back and to offer a rich environment. At the beginning we should focus on the spoken language and support it in Children’s house through the activities that we offer. Language is a tool for communication and self-expression.

Order is a part of our life and we as humans tend to seek it even in the everyday life. While talking about order for the child, Maria Montessori talked about the child as a new comer in the world who has to make sense of the environment that surrounds him. It is trough external order that the child can build the internal order. Maria Montessori said that the sensitive period for order is one of the most important but yet mysterious. The children in the sensitive period for order have a love for order. The sensitive period for order is very important for the acquisition for language.

children.title: Refinement of the senses (Birth to 6 years old)

blocks.text: All the impressions that we perceive come through our senses. The senses play an important part in the connection with the environment in which child is raised. Maria Montessori acknowledged this sensitivity and created a prepared environment for the young child to support this sensitive period. At home the child should be allowed as well to continue exploring and to develop.

It is the tiny, the diminutive objects/details that attract the child in this period. The child is exploring the environment at this stage and learns from what surrounds him. It’s a short period but maybe its role is to develop a capacity to discern detail.

The coordinated movement is something that has to be constructed and developed. In respect for this period of movement in the Children’s house there are prepared activities to aid the child in the development. Purposeful activity for the child comes from the inner drive to develop and it is not driven by the

final goal of reaching the end of the activity but the goal is the development itself. For the development of the coordinated movement in Children’s house there are many activities in the Practical Life that support the coordination of the movement, eye-hand coordination and the equilibrium/balance.

The family is the nucleus for the development of the social behavior in the first two-three years of life. By the time the child goes to the Children’s House the mixed age environment supports the development in this sensitive period. The child wants to be part of their culture and it is interested how he can interact and behave with the others.

These sensitive periods are not just for learning as some might point out, the final goal is development not only learning. Yet it is there to say that during these sensitive periods the child will learn with facility and ease. These sensitive originate in the child, the prepared environment supports the development of the child meanwhile an inappropriate environment might hinder the development.

The knowledge of these sensitive periods is why in the Children’s House there is no fixed timetable. Each child is allowed to spend as long as needed with a particular activity. This knowledge of the sensitive periods should be observed and acknowledged at home as well as at school.

“These periods correspond to special sensibilities to be found in creatures in the process of development; they are transitory and confined to the acquisition of a determined characteristic. Once this characteristic has evolved, the corresponding
sensibility disappears. Thus every characteristic is established by the help of an impulse, of a transient sensibility which lasts over a limited period of growth” Maria
Montessori – Secret of childhood
It is very important for us as adults to recognize the sensitivities of a child and support them.

The adult should never forget that he/she is a constant role model. The appearance, movement, language and care should be cared about as the child in the first plane of development has a desire to look-up at the adult in the group and absorb what he/she sees.

In the Children’s House there are a few specific activities that support the development of the social behavior for example: “Grace and Courtesy”, “Walking on the line”, “The silent game”, “The bank game”, etc.
Maria Montessori said that an adapted human being wants to benefit the other persons outside of his immediate group.

“To animals perfection of movement is giving by nature, and the grace of the tiger or the squirrel is due to the wealth of opposition put into play to attain that harmony. In man this mechanism, is not there at birth, so has to be created, and this is done by
practical experiences in the environment. It is not so much exercise of movement, but of co-ordination. This co-ordination is not fixed for the human child, but has to be
created and perfected through the psyche” Maria Montessori – Education for a New World

Human movement it is not so fixed as in the movement of the animals, it has more like an open-end. All humans have their particular way to move. Co-ordination for the movement it is very important for the life of a human being. The upright posture is very specific for the human as well as the use of the hand for working. The development of the equilibrium is gradual but pretty fixed. The development of equilibrium depends of the process of myelination and the development of the cerebellum. At 2 months the child starts turning his head to follow the voice, at 3-4 months the child rolls from their tummy to their back. Around the age of 6 months he is able to sit. At approximately 7 months the child can roll from the back to the tummy. Later around 8 months the child starts crawling, around 10 months the child begins to stand and at 12 months the child starts walking. Crawling is a very important sign of independence for the child as he is now able to move around by himself. With walking it comes even a greater grade of independence. Equilibrium is a state of balance, of being in harmony with oneself and with the surroundings.
It is the use of the hand that is very important in connecting us with the environment. Once the child can stand up he can start using the hands.

Around 18 months old the child as described by Dr. Maria Montessori enters in a period of Maximum effort, he walks carrying heavy objects – as a way to gain more strength. The child will try to use movement to get to know their environment and to develop its movement capacities already acquired. It is a characteristic of the man to think with his hands. The hands are the most important tool of the human being.
“Motor development and cognitive development may be much more interrelated that has been previously appreciated. Indeed, they may be fundamentally intertwined” Adele Diamond, 2000
Maria Montessori pointed out from the beginning, the close connection of the developing mind with movement.

The language acquisition is a gradual process, the child is not born with any premeditated language but with the capacity to construct any language. The two main function of language are communication and maintaining relationships and a tool for cognition. The children develop the language with the help of the absorbent mind.
“A baby so enjoys the divine music of the human voice that he will ignore other noises” Maria Montessori – The 1946 London Lectures

At the beginning, there is a big disproportion between the receptive organs and the productive organs. The fact that the child is not talking it does not mean that he does not understand or that there is no process going on. From a very young age, the child will turn the head to follow the mouth that speaks. At around 6 months, the child start to babble. All the children around the world make the same babbling sounds, but later they retain only the sounds that are typical for the child’s language. Babbling strengthens the tongue, lips and the mouth – we should allow the child to do it and not suppress it. At the age of 10 months, the child start to link sounds, and at the age of one the child will say the first intentional name. The first words of the child are usually nouns or names.

At around 18 months, the child’s vocabulary will have many nouns and will start forming phrases without meaning. Around the age of 2 the child will enter in an explosive epoch where he completes the vocabulary with prefixes, suffixes, conjunctions, verbs, conjugations and adverbs. Between the age of 2 and 2 and a half the variety of phrases increases rapidly, now he will be using the coordinated, subordinated phrases with the subjunctive.
The spoken language develops as if the child is hungry for words. The environment at home and at school has to be rich in words to support this hunger of words and offer the exact words.
