Writing is easier than reading, this is why it comes earlier. Writing requires a lower level of abstraction than reading, as writing is just a manner of self-expression, of concepts with which the child is already comfortable with.
Independence is the ability to think for yourself and do things for yourself.

Everything in the society starts from one-self capacity to be independent, even if our society is one interdependent. All the developmental processes depend on the experiences that the child has with the group and the environment but still the process itself is an independent one.

The child always strives for independence but it does not mean that the environment it is always favorable for it. This is why it is important for the adult to create an environment that encourages and helps the child to become independent.

Maria Montessori said that the first sign of independence it is the moment of birth itself. In the first 6 months, the child is very attached to the mother but from the moment the first teeth appear it is the moment when they start becoming more independent for food. At 1 year old the child starts to walk independently and he can move freely in the environment. At 18 months, the children walk, as they want to strengthen their muscles, practice walking and explore the environment that surrounds them. The child should be allowed to participate in the daily life, do things by himself and to express himself.

In Children’s House independence it is at the heart of how the prepared environment is organized. It is an environment that supports this need of the child to become independent meanwhile he can develop and find activities of this interest.

If the child develops independence from a young age it is very probable that this behavior will stay with the child for his whole life. Even if the independence is not something that stays constant during one’s life it is something that all the human beings strive for.
For a child’s independence the adult should give the child time, allow him to participate, help when only necessary and create an accessible environment.
“And so we discovered, that education it is not something that the teacher does, but that it is a natural process that develops spontaneously in the human being, It is
not acquired by listening to words, but in virtue of experiences in which the child acts on his environment”
Maria Montessori – The absorbent mind

The prepared environment it is present in all the education plans in the Montessori approach to education. For a plant to grow it requires soil, light, water and carbon– dioxide so as the human being requires a specific environment to develop properly. For the environment we should not only think of the psychic aspect but also the spiritual and social one. When talking about an environment for the child we must have in mind the developmental needs of the child at a respective age.
The first environment for a child is the mother’s womb where he gets everything he needs.
During the first plane the child’s own tasks are adaptation and self-construction.
The child should have a prepared environment at home as well as at school. The

environment at home should contain an area for sleeping, an area for self-care, an area for eating and another one for play and activity. Making these areas accessible for the child helps the child to become independent and help himself whenever he needs something (E.g. eating a snack, dress himself, getting out the bed, etc.). The adults should help the children learn how to do the things for themselves, offer limited choices, encourage the child to put the items back to their place when finished and allow time.
Beside the prepared environment, the adults should have some consistent routines for the child and clear expectations which allow the child to feel safe and secure of this actions.
The prepared environment in Children’s House offers opportunities for the co-

ordination of movement, language, independence, repetition, concentration, problem solving, refinement of the senses, social development and to explore the world culture. In the prepared environment the children are offered the opportunity to explore by themselves and are not taught.

The environment should be beautiful, aesthetically pleasing as this supports the development of care for the environment, respect for the materials and allows the child to develop its good taste. Beauty also inspires activity in the environment.

Order is very important in the environment. Everything has a place in the environment, the materials are ordered from simple to complex, like things are grouped together and colour coded. The order it is not only about the physical environment but also the consistency with which the adults act in the environment.
The materials, objects and furniture is child-sized to foster the independence and as a sign of respect for them as persons.
The activities are all real and no pretend – activities as we want the child to experience the real and use it for his developmental needs.

children.title: Purposeful hands-on activities with control of error

blocks.text: These activities besides being real are also purposeful hands-on experiences which have a control of error to allow the child to overcome challenges independently and have a friendlier attitude towards mistakes.
Harmony is another aspect of the Children’s House environment, harmony in the way we interact with each other in the community.

The activities in the Children’s House are grouped in: practical life materials, sensorial materials, language materials, mathematics materials and the culture materials (the world, plants, animals, art, music and science).

In the practical life area there are activities that deal with the care of oneself and care of the environment. The daily life activities give opportunities to develop co- ordinated movement, independence, concentration and an “I can do it” attitude. There are group activities such as “Grace and Courtesy”, “Walking on the line” and the “Silence game”.
The activities in the sensorial area help the child to get a refined sensory perception, organize and classify the impressions received.

In the language area the activities help the child to enrich his vocabulary, improve his self-expression, communicate with the adults and their peers and to express himself. Oral expression, writing and reading are key strands of the language activities in the Children’s House.

For the mathematics area the materials help the children to grasp mathematical concepts through concrete hands on experience. There is a gradual progression from concrete to abstract. This allows the children to discover with a lot of joy the mathematics and have a clear understanding.
The culture area is a gate for the knowledge and understand of the world.
An outdoor environment is an important part of the Children’s House environment and it should follow as much as possible the same rules as the indoor environment.
For enhancing the progression in the most beneficial way for the child some principles must be followed:

The freedom in the Children’s house goes hand in hand with the responsibility. One of the key freedoms that are offered is the freedom of choice. The child is able to choose activities that are developmental appropriate at that time.
The freedom of time is important to allow the children develop and satisfy their developmental needs as long as necessary.
Freedom of movement in the environment is offered to allow the child to explore and observe.

Limits or boundaries are always present in the Children’s House. The material is limited, one of each, encouraging the children to be respectful, take turns and learn to be patient. There is respect for the work of another, where children can join an activity only if the other invited. Returning the work back it is important as a sign of finalising an activity and also helps with the order and independence in environment.
In the environment it is very important that a classroom is of mixed age which will help the children to function like in a mini-society, care of the others and take responsibility.

The environment should take in consideration the absorbent mind of the child, his sensitivities of the child corresponding to the plane of development in which the child is. It is really important to appreciate that it is not only about the physical space, but to put the principles into practice.
The role of the adult is to prepare the environment, ensure that the environment functions according to the freedoms, principles and boundaries giving clear
exceptions to the child. Other responsibility of the adult is to help and connect the child to the environment and to observe and respond accordingly.
“The love for one’s environment is the secret of all man’s progress and the secret of social evolution” Maria Montessori – Education and peace

children.title: Montessori teacher – The role of the adult

blocks.text: “Our goal is not so much the imparting of knowledge as the unveiling and developing of spiritual knowledge” Maria Montessori - The child in the family
When Maria Montessori talked about the teacher, she referred to it like “la maestra”, now around the world the role of the teacher is called directress, director or guide.
“… the adult must pass from the role of commanding creator to be obeyed to a role of a scientist who studies how best he can help the process of developing life.” AMI
Communications 2002

The roles of the Montessori teacher are to prepare and maintain the environment, to connect the child to the environment and to observe. It is very important to take very good care of the environment, make sure it is complete, clean and attractive for the children.

It is the task of the teacher to demonstrate to the child the use of the material and what material should be introduced to a child depending on his interests and developmental needs. Once presented the material it is important for the teacher to know when to step back and let the child work with the material independently and guard the child’s focus. The teacher must intervene when the child is misusing the material.
Child
Teacher Environment

The teacher must observe the environment, see it’s doing it function, observe the children working, the developmental moment of each child and also very important is to observe how the teacher’s team is functioning in the classroom.
A teacher’s preparation has to include the intellectual preparation, physical preparation and the spiritual preparation.

It is very important for the Montessori teacher to understand the developmental planes, the sensitivities of the child and the human tendencies. The knowledge of the Montessori materials is very important, the connections, the fundamental principles of the material, the aims and the inter-relationships between different materials. The practice with the materials is very important as there is no other way to get to know and be familiar with their use and inter-relationships.
A teacher must be a person with a good general knowledge about the world.

The teacher’s appearance has to have a clean and attractive professional appearance, without using bright/saturated colours. No jewellery or other accessories that might distract the attention of the children.
The spiritual preparation it is very important for how we interact and view the child. At the end of the day the only person that we can change it is our self.

The teacher should never label the children, she should avoid prejudice and look at the children with fresh eyes. The teacher should be like a gardener, to offer the proper conditions for growth every day.
“So this school is both for the teacher and for the child” Maria Montessori
“To gain knowledge one must study, but to gain wisdom one must observe” Unknown author – Ashram in India
Observation is the act of looking at something with close attention and care for the details.

The observation has to be objective and neutral without getting into any conclusions. While observing the child must not be aware that you are observing him as this might be distracting for him or force him to be behave in a different way. The data collected should be organized in a clear and chronological way without any preliminary conclusions. Without observation we cannot know the likes, challenges and individual developmental needs at one moment of the child.
Observation is very different from the record tracking. Observation should take in account the emotional, cognitive, physical and social development of the individual.
Emotional Cognitive
Physical Social

“To her falls the task of guiding the development of the child’s spirit, and therefore her observation are not limited solely to understanding him. All her observations must emerge at the end – and this is their only justification – in her ability to help the child”
Maria Montessori – The child in the family
Maria Montessori talked about how vital is to take the time to observe the child and to guide the steps which are to come on the base of this observation of the individual development of the child.

Observation it is not only for an individual child, but also can be used to observe the whole group and the team of teachers. This valuable observation time can be used later to reflect and try to find solutions for some of the issues identified earlier.

In the Montessori pedagogy, the concepts of freedom and discipline come hand in hand. A concept of freedom is at the heart of humanity and the human being is constantly seeking it. We seek it as individuals and nations as well.
The more independent a person is the higher grade of freedom he can exercise.
“No one can be free if he is not independent. Therefore the active manifestations of personal liberty must be guided from earliest infancy.” Maria Montessori - Absorbent
mind
The punishment – rewards system doesn’t help an individual to become an independent and freer person.

“No-one, who has ever done anything great or successful, has ever done it simply because he was attracted by what we call a “reward” or by the fear of what we call punishment… Every victory and every advance in human progress comes from
some inner compulsion” Maria Montessori – Discovery of the child

The Children’s House tries to foster the self-discipline through engagement to support the child’s development and adaptation. This can be done by offering the child rich motives for activity, activities that respond to the child’s development, activities offered in the way that they are of interest and appealing to the child.

The principles and functioning of the prepared environment are freedoms with limits, individualized instruction, uninterrupted work cycle, mixed age groups and control of error. The freedoms offered are: choice, time, movement, activity/work, to be and to be observe.

The freedom of choice is a sign of respect for the child and an empowerment to help the child follow its own interests and supports the development of the child as it allows to repeat an activity as long as he wants. Without experience and knowledge the child cannot make choices as they don’t what they can do – here the role of the guide is crucial. Having a mixed age group helps also the younger children to get inspired by the activities done by the others in the group and make their choices based on what their friends are doing.

The freedom of time it is an aid for the self-development of each child, allowing him to work as long as necessary to for a specific ability/sensibility. It also support the concentration of the child allowing him to focus on a task without being interrupted.

The freedom of movement it is an aid for the independence of the child, supports the human tendency to explore as it allows the child to explore his own environment. It gives the option to observe the other children’s work and absorb from what the others are doing.

The freedom of activity/work it is empowering the independence and self-choice, help the child feel that he is respected in the group. It allows the child to follow his interests and to choose activities that pose a challenge. They are free do the work independently on in a group.
The freedom to communicate is very important for the child especially in the first plane of development when his language passes through a stage of construction and later on of refinement.

The freedom to be/to observe allows the child to observe his colleagues, to take his own time to reflect on some of the things that considers important and just to feel free to have a rest if he feels he needs one.
“Work is the cornerstone of freedom. The freedom of our children has as its limit the community, for freedom does not mean doing what one wants, but being master of
oneself” Maria Montessori

One of each material is an important concept for the prepared environment as it helps the children to appreciate the materials, helps the children to gain patience and to take turns. When a desired material is not available it puts the child in a situation in which he has to make a choice.

children.title: Respecting the work of the others

blocks.text: Respecting the work of the others is an important principle not only in the prepared environment but as well in the society that the children will encounter outside of the classroom. Respecting this principle teaches respect not only for the others work but also for their person.

Returning the work back to the shelf supports the sensibility for order in the environment, helping the children not only to keep the environment tidy but also helps the others to orientate in the environment when all the works are in their own place.
“To let the child do as he likes when he has not yet developed any powers of
control, would be to betray the idea of freedom” Maria
Montessori – Absorbent mind
All the limits and freedoms are there to show the children that all the choices impact the others in the group.
The children are not afraid to make mistakes as built in control of error encourages
repetition and perseverance in overcoming a difficulty.
The built in control of error allows the child to be independent and auto-educate
himself and judge for himself instead of getting the validation/criticism from the others.
First level of obedience: the child will do what you ask for and sometimes not because maybe they are not able to do it
Second level of obedience: the children will obey your requests but they will not show any satisfaction from doing it.
Third level of obedience: when the children obey because they want to be of service to someone.

“Another interesting phenomena which comes is obedience. We think of freedom and obedience as being two contracting things. Instead these free children are singularly obedient. Obedience must come from the formation of an individual. Otherwise it is a repression.” Maria Montessori – Child, Society and the World
It is an inner force that keeps the humans going, moving towards a particular action: persevering. Values and self-control cannot be taught, they develop only through self- experience.

Our lives are in constant connection with the others, the child needs the presence of other humans. The first child’s social group is family, so that the child has a feel of safety, love and care. It is very important that in the family the children get the rules of behaviour (code of conduct). The child should be able to be part in the life of the family. At around 2.5 years old the children’s need a broader social environment, in some cultures the children go to kindergarten or play groups.
The absorbent mind help the children to absorb the social environment and around this age the children have a sensitive period for the social behaviour.
Maria Montessori called the child in the second half of the first plane of development (3-6) called the child a social embryo.

This social development it is supported in the Children’s House environment with a mixed-age group. They are grouped depending on the developmental needs of the children (they are in the same plane of development).

The benefits of a mixed-age group are that children develop respect for the others and their activity, are exposed to a wide range of activities, the younger children learn by observing the older children, the older children have the opportunity to validate their knowledge by helping the younger, they develop in a non-competitive environment, it reflects the real community, fewer adults as the children can work and organize their community.

A mixed aged group besides of being non-competitive, it is a stable group in which the children can develop and take responsibilities with the time. It allows the children to have enough time to know each other better and appreciate more one another. A unique space of independence and interdependence.
“the most important single result of our whole work” Maria Montessori – Absorbent mind

Maria Montessori used the word deviation as getting away from the normal path of development, meanwhile the word normalization refers to the normal path of development. Normalization is a developmental stage which reveals the child’s true nature. Maria Montessori said that this process is only possible in a supportive environment. The teacher in the Children’s House has normalization as a goal for his overall work. Some of the characteristics of a normalized child are concentration, love of work, self- discipline, sociability and some of deviations identified by Maria Montessori are caprice, disorder, timidity, laziness, fear, lying, etc. Maria Montessori talks about the super social child as a desirable characteristic of the child who is empathetic, helps others and shows self-control. Meanwhile the extra- social child is the one who is not yet able to control themselves. To support the normalization it is important to direct our attention towards the prepared environment, remove the obstacles from the environment, facilitate individual and social experiences, help the children to develop their character and ensure that they are part of a mixed-age group which corresponds to their plan of development. We can look at the characteristics of the normalized child as a goal but also as a mean.

“But when the attractions of the new environment exert their spell, offering motives for constructive activity, then all these energies combine and deviations can be dispersed. A unique type of child appears, a “new child”; but really it is the child’s true “personality” allowed to construct itself normally.” Maria Montessori – Absorbent mind
Practical life activities are daily life activities necessary for the independence of the young child.

The key tasks of the child in the first plane of development are adaptation, self- construction and the creation of the personality. The practical life activities respond to the child’s development as these activities are based on the human tendencies and the absorbent mind. It is important to mention that these activities support the adaption of the child and the development of the sensitivities of the child (language, order, coordinated movement and social behavior).
The practical life activities are like a bridge between the school environment and home as the child might see these activities at home performed by the adults.
“…no other occupations which could be undertaken by the children at this stage, could be more important for their whole development – physical, mental and moral
than these “exercises of practical life” as they are called” E.M.Standing – Maria Montessori, Her work and her life
The purposes of the practical life activities are coordinated movement, independence and concentration – some also have as purpose the social behavior.
“The child seeks for independence by means of work, an independence of body and mind” Maria Montessori – The absorbent mind

For the child to concentrate while using the practical life materials the adult must ensure that the child has an interest for that activity, he is free to choose, is allowed to do it by himself as long as he needs and as many times as he desires.

It is important to mention the features of the practical life activities, these activities have to be attractive, functional, breakable, always complete, purposeful, child-sized, culture specific and seasonal. Having attractive materials invites the child to use it and care about it. The functional aspect of the material is very important to support the development of the child and avoid the frustration that a half-functional material might cause. Breakable materials increase the concentration and increase the care the children take of the items.
The practical life activities should have a real purpose and be culture-specific to resemble activities that the child can do in his home environment.
The environment is prepared from simple to complex, similar activities are group together and colour coded so that the child can put them back without the help of the adult.
Most of the activities in the practical life are individual activities, even though there some group activities such as “Grace and Courtesy”, “Walking on the line” and “The silence game”.

The preliminary activities are activities that help the children how to function in the environment: “how to roll a mat”, “how to carry a chair”, etc. and activities that help the children to do other activities in the future: “open/closing”, “folding” etc.
The care of the person activities which help the child to become more independent and take care of himself: “washing the hands”, “dressing frames”, etc.
The care of the environment activities are important to empower the children to take care of the environment that surrounds them at school and at home: “dusting”, “watering the plants”, etc.
These activities impart coordinated movement, independence and social behavior development.

Grace and courtesy activities teach the children how to address in the society, deal gracefully with the situations that may present in the daily life (E.g. introduce themselves, ask for something or even refuse something).
Some grace and courtesy activities might address the movement in the environment, handling of the materials or the furniture.
A child who knows the norms of grace and courtesy of the group he will feel proud, independent and have a sense of belonging to the group.

The children with the help of this activity develop their coordinated movement, balance, equilibrium and self-control. For this activity a meandering line it is recommended if the activity is carried indoors and an ellipse if the activity is carried outdoors and faster steps and skipping is used.
The silent game is used to help the children to develop self-control. While doing this activity the children will gain a sense of joy, achievement and social spirit.
"One day I had the idea of using silence to test the children's keenness of hearing, so I thought of calling them by name, in a low whisper.... This exercise in patient waiting
demanded a patience that I thought impossible." —Maria Montessori, The Secret of Childhood

It is the adult’s responsibility to prepare the activity, present it to the child, observe the child’s activity and to help the child put the activity away when the child is done only if the child requires help.

The practical life activities benefit the development of the individual as well as the group, the effort is collective which brings responsibility and the children can contribute each of them depending on their capacity, it creates a space of cooperation and collaboration. “We must understand that the exercises of practical life are not intended as training

of practical skills. They are a kind of gymnastic training for the harmonious development of the psychic and motor parts of the individual. The individual becomes a unity so that a movement is not just a movement of the hand but of the
whole person.” Maria Montessori - !946 London Lectures
The senses are the gate through which the absorbent mind can construct itself, as all the information the brain gathers comes through the senses.
The sensorial materials support the sensitive periods of the first plane child and help him refine his senses, gain language and support the social behaviour.
The senses are enormously important for the human beings in the daily life as everything we do it has to use one or some of the senses in connection.

“If training of this sort is undertaken at an age when the formative periods naturally over, it will be difficult and imperfect. The secret of preparing one for a particular skill consists in utilising that period of life between the ages of three and six , when there is a natural inclination to perfect one’s senses and movements” Maria Montessori –
Discovery of the child

The sensorial materials enable the mind to organise, order and classify the stream of impressions the child is receiving from the environment, refine the senses, build a store of abstract concepts, increase the perception of the world, build the intelligence, give a foundation for future learning and help to discover some possible problems with the development of the child.
The sensorial materials have all or some of the following characteristics:
The materials isolate one quality, allowing the child to focus on one difficulty at a time.
Young children learn through their senses and it is important to isolate a sense in the material, as this will allow the child to concentrate and develop that particular sense.
The materials are made from natural materials, glass, metal and wood and are beautifully painted to attract the child to work with it and take of the material.

The Montessori materials are scientifically designed to offer not only a direct preparation necessary at the moment when the child works with the material but also to prepare him indirectly for more advanced concepts.
In the Montessori classroom, there is only one copy of each material.
All the materials allow the child to work actively with the material – a “hands-on” learning approach.

Some of the materials in the classroom prepare the child for further activities in Elementary school. (E.g. the binomial cube it is a sensorial experience in Children’s House and it is used in Elementary to demonstrate the formula (a+b)2
Some materials have included an control of error, allowing the child to work independently and avoid the frustration of being corrected by someone else.
For the initial presentations there are many benefits of presenting the contrasts first to help the child with the sensorial discrimination and to show sometimes the range.
Another process used is identities, for some of the works the children have to pair or sort similar qualities (fabric box, second box of colour tablets, baric tablets, etc.).
The process of gradation comes later as it is more difficult for the child (E.g. third colour box).
The process of offering the language to the child comes almost at last, after the child had the sensorial experience.
The sensorial games are played in small groups after all the children have the sensorial and language experience with the material used in the game (E.g. matching the sound boxes at a distance).
Most of the sensorial materials, have an initial presentation and a few following exercises which will allow the repetition of the work with the same material.
“The hand touches the evidence and the mind discovers the secret” Maria Montessori – Psychogeometry
